title: The Everglades: Wowee
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Jerry) explore the Everglades in southern Florida: its geography and boundaries, the Seminole name Pahayokee and early naming, the limestone bedrock and Biscayne Aquifer, the hydrology linking Lake Okeechobee to the slow-moving river of grass, the Native American peoples who lived there (Tequesta, Calusa, Ais, Seminole, Miccosukee), early drainage and canal building, conservation pioneers Ernest F. Coe and Marjorie Stoneman Douglas, the 1947 national park, the Central and Southern Florida Project after the 1947 hurricane, the nine ecosystems (hardwood hammocks, pine rocklands, sloughs, marl prairies, cypress, mangroves, coastal lowlands, Florida Bay), wildlife such as alligators, crocodiles, Florida panthers, manatees and birds, the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan and the US Sugar land buyback collapse, climate change, and listener mail from an AP English class at Wasco High School.

entities.name: Central and Southern Florida Project for Flood Control and Other Purposes

segments.title: Live tour dates promo
segments.summary: Hosts announce 2024 live tour dates and where to get tickets.

segments.title: Opening banter and pharma ads
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about pharmaceutical commercials and introduce the Everglades topic.

segments.title: Chuck's airboat trip and Okefenokee memories
segments.summary: Chuck describes a recent airboat tour in the Everglades with a guide named Kenny and compares it to a past trip to the Okefenokee Swamp, focusing on birds.

segments.title: What and where the Everglades are
segments.summary: Josh defines the Everglades as a patchwork of ecosystems on southern Florida, from below Orlando to the Florida Keys, bounded by high ground from Palm Beach to Miami. Chuck notes the Seminole name Pahayokee meaning grassy waters, and that 'Everglades' first appeared on a map in 1823. Josh explains the word glade and describes sawgrass sloughs.

segments.title: Airboats, swamp buggies and grass recovery
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how airboats and swamp buggies disturb the marsh, and how sawgrass tracks recover.

segments.title: Everglades National Park versus the wider Everglades
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh clarify that the national park covers only part of the larger Everglades region.

segments.title: Florida natural history: limestone, aquifer and water flow
segments.summary: Josh explains Florida's limestone bedrock formed from ancient seabeds, the Biscayne Aquifer supplying drinking water to millions, and the very gentle elevation slope. The Atlantic Coastal Ridge holds water in the Everglades. Lake Okeechobee floods south over thousands of years, and accumulated shell and mud forms a natural dam. Water percolates slowly into the aquifer. Florida Bay is about five feet deep.

segments.title: Indigenous peoples of the Everglades
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss the indigenous peoples who settled southern Florida, including the Tequesta, Ais, and Calusa, and the Seminole and Miccosukee who formed from displaced groups and fugitives who hid in the Everglades.

segments.title: Early settlers call the land valueless
segments.summary: Europeans first considered the Everglades worthless swamp; the first state legislature called it valueless and set out to drain it. Florida was acquired from Spain in 1819 by treaty.

segments.title: Early canals and drainage
segments.summary: Canals and ditches were dug to divert water from Lake Okeechobee to rivers and the Atlantic, reducing flooding of farmland and towns but cutting the Everglades off from its main water source.

segments.title: Early conservation: Ernest F. Coe and Marjorie Stoneman Douglas
segments.summary: In the 1920s some people began objecting to the damage. Land developer Ernest F. Coe campaigned for a national park, which was established in 1947. Journalist Marjorie Stoneman Douglas later wrote The Everglades: River of Grass, which shifted public attitudes toward protection. Governor Napoleon Bonaparte Broward is mentioned in connection with tourism and birds.

segments.title: Park size and the shrinking Everglades
segments.summary: The national park is about 1.5 million acres, roughly an eighth of the historical Everglades, which once covered about 18,000 square miles. Real estate development and agriculture around Lake Okeechobee have further reduced it.

segments.title: Hurricanes, flood control and the Central and Southern Florida Project
segments.summary: After the 1947 hurricane, Congress authorized the Central and Southern Florida Project for Flood Control and Other Purposes in 1948. Canals and levees continue to divert about 1.7 billion gallons of water a day to the Atlantic and Gulf.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: The nine habitats of the Everglades
segments.summary: The National Park Service divides the Everglades into nine habitats. Hardwood hammocks are tree islands formed by roots capturing dirt. Pine rocklands are fire-dependent forests found only in South Florida and the Bahamas. Freshwater sloughs such as Shark River Slough and Taylor Slough are sawgrass rivers. Marl prairies are calcium-rich ecosystems, and cypress and mangrove forests appear too.

segments.title: Mangroves, coastal lowlands and Florida Bay
segments.summary: Mangroves protect against storms and the Everglades has the largest contiguous mangrove ecosystem in the Western Hemisphere. Coastal lowlands are scrub desert, and Florida Bay is a shallow fishing area included in the national park.

segments.title: Wildlife: alligators, crocodiles, panthers, manatees
segments.summary: Florida is the only place with both alligators and crocodiles, with about 200,000 alligators and about 2,000 crocodiles. American crocodiles were around 200 in 1975. Florida panther numbers rose from 20 to 30 in the 1970s to about 200. Manatees declined from sea grass loss and algae die-offs linked to Lake Okeechobee discharges, and were fed lettuce and cabbage.

segments.title: Birds, butterflies and orchids
segments.summary: Chuck describes birds including roseate spoonbills and cranes seen on the airboat tour, and Emily's birding app. Josh recommends the magazine Birds and Blooms. They mention butterflies and a possible future episode on orchids.

segments.title: Everglades Restoration Plan and US Sugar buyback
segments.summary: UNESCO listed the Everglades as a World Heritage Site in 1979. Congress passed the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan in 2000, projected at eight billion dollars over twenty years but slow to be funded. A planned purchase of about 180,000 acres from US Sugar for about 1.75 billion dollars collapsed after the 2008 financial crisis.

segments.title: Peat, climate change and restoration challenges
segments.summary: Peat forms from organic material without oxygen and can release carbon if the wetland dries. The restoration plan did not account for climate change. Josh recommends articles from Fizz and an NPR interview with Jenny Staletovich.

segments.title: Listener mail from Wasco High School AP English class
segments.summary: Chuck reads emails from an AP English class at Wasco High School whose teacher assigned them to listen to the show and send listener mail. Hosts shout out many students.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the listener mail address and sign off.
